items.q: Is carbon ion therapy better than proton therapy for my cancer?
items.a: Not necessarily. Carbon ions have a higher biological effect and may be preferred for selected radioresistant tumours such as chordoma, chondrosarcoma, and some sarcomas, while proton therapy is often better suited to paediatric cancers, brain tumours, and prostate cancer where sparing healthy tissue is the priority. Neither is universally superior — the right choice depends on your exact diagnosis, tumour location, and prior treatment, and should be made by a radiation oncology team after full review.

items.q: Carbon ion therapy is not available in India. What are my realistic options?
items.a: India offers advanced radiotherapy including IMRT, IGRT, SBRT, stereotactic radiosurgery, and proton therapy at the Apollo Proton Cancer Centre in Chennai, while carbon ion therapy is generally accessed abroad in countries such as Japan, Germany, China, Italy, or Austria. The most useful first step is usually an expert review to confirm whether carbon ion therapy is genuinely needed or whether proton therapy, SBRT, or another option in India would serve equally well. This should be assessed on a case-by-case basis.

items.q: Which cancers are most suitable for carbon ion therapy?
items.a: The most established indications are skull base chordoma and chondrosarcoma, and selected bone and soft tissue sarcomas, since these tumours are often radioresistant and located near critical structures. It is also considered for some recurrent cancers and selected head and neck, prostate, liver, and pancreatic tumours. Suitability always has to be confirmed by a specialist, since the same diagnosis can be appropriate for one patient and not another depending on stage and prior treatment.

items.q: Can carbon ion therapy cure my cancer?
items.a: In selected localised cancers, carbon ion therapy may be given with the intent to cure; in others, it is used to control the tumour locally or relieve symptoms. Whether cure is realistic depends on cancer type, stage, and whether disease has spread, since carbon ion therapy is a local treatment and cannot address cancer elsewhere in the body. A responsible treatment centre will give a realistic picture of what it can achieve for your specific case rather than a guaranteed outcome.

items.q: I had radiation before. Can I still have carbon ion therapy?
items.a: Sometimes, yes — in selected patients, carbon ion therapy's precision may allow re-irradiation that would be too risky with standard techniques, but this is never routine. It can only be assessed safely if your previous radiation dose and treatment plans are available for review, so the team can judge how much additional dose nearby tissue can tolerate. Keeping complete copies of prior radiation records is important for this evaluation.

items.q: What side effects does carbon ion therapy cause?
items.a: Side effects depend on the treatment site but commonly include localized skin reaction, fatigue, and site-specific effects such as difficulty swallowing for head and neck tumours or bowel changes for pelvic tumours. Because the beam is highly precise, side effects to distant healthy tissue are generally more limited than with older radiation techniques, though they are not eliminated. Your treatment team will monitor and manage side effects throughout the course of therapy.

items.q: How long does a course of carbon ion therapy take?
items.a: Treatment schedules vary by centre, tumour type, and protocol, but carbon ion therapy is often given over a shorter overall course than conventional radiation — commonly around four sessions a week for up to about four weeks. The exact number of sessions and total duration is determined by the treatment planning team based on your specific tumour and treatment goal. International patients should confirm the expected schedule in advance for travel planning.

items.q: Is carbon ion therapy painful, and does it require anesthesia?
items.a: The treatment itself is not painful — patients do not feel the beam during delivery, similar to having an X-ray. Some patients require an immobilization mask or frame to stay perfectly still, and in select cases such as young children, light sedation may be used for positioning. Any discomfort typically relates to side effects that develop over the course of treatment rather than the sessions themselves.

items.q: How much does carbon ion therapy cost compared to proton therapy?
items.a: Carbon ion therapy is typically more expensive than proton therapy, reflecting the smaller number of centres worldwide and the complexity of the technology, though exact costs vary significantly by country, centre, and treatment plan. A firm cost estimate can only be given after a centre reviews your diagnosis, imaging, and treatment plan. Comparing the total cost against proton therapy or other options is worth doing as part of an initial case review.

items.q: How does CancerFax help patients considering carbon ion therapy?
items.a: CancerFax helps patients organize medical reports, imaging, pathology, and any previous radiation records, then coordinates an expert review to assess whether carbon ion therapy, proton therapy, or another option may be suitable, along with travel and logistics support. CancerFax is a navigation platform, not a hospital, and does not make treatment decisions — those are made by the treating radiation oncology team after reviewing your full case.
